Short close front vowel [i], stressed in the Greek form.
Velar nasal [ŋ] before the final stop.
Voiceless velar stop [k] plus voiceless sibilant [s], the standard ending.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SFINGKS' — aspirate the 'p' as you release it, stress the first syllable, and end with a sharp 'ks'.

kin.label: Egyptian
kin.form: The Great Sphinx at Giza, a guardian lion with human head, predates the Greek myth by millennia.

kin.label: Modern
kin.form: The word 'sphinx' has become a synonym for any enigma or riddling presence.

pronunciation.note: The PUNICODEX form Sphigx restores the Greek consonant cluster γξ as gx, matching the scholarly transliteration of Σφίγξ. The more common English spelling 'Sphinx' flattens the gamma to n; the Sphigx form keeps the etymological strangling cluster visible.

domains.title: Riddling Monster
domains.subtitle: Guardian, Strangler, and Threshold Terror
domains.lead: The Sphinx is the winged lion-woman who crouched outside Thebes and strangled those who could not answer her riddle. She is not merely a monster but a guardian of thresholds: the creature who bars entry until the traveller proves worthy of understanding.

cards.name: Guardian of Thebes
cards.desc: She perched on a cliff and posed a riddle to every traveller.

cards.name: The Riddle
cards.desc: 'What walks on four feet in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening?'

cards.name: Strangler
cards.desc: Her name means 'the strangling one'; she killed all who failed.

cards.name: Defeated by Oedipus
cards.desc: Oedipus answered 'man'; she leaped to her death in shame.

symbols.name: Lion's body
symbols.meaning: Royal power and the dangerous strength of the threshold guardian.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: The aerial, predatory nature of the creature; she strikes from above.

symbols.name: Woman's head
symbols.meaning: Intelligence and speech, the source of the deadly riddle.

symbols.name: Cliff or gate
symbols.meaning: The liminal place between safety and destruction.

mythology.lead: The Greek Sphinx is a daughter of monstrous parents, sent by Hera to punish Thebes. Her story is inseparable from the tragedy of Oedipus.

myths.title: Child of Echidna and Typhon
myths.text: The Sphinx was born from Echidna, the half-woman half-serpent, and Typhon, the storm-giant who once challenged Zeus. Her siblings included Cerberus, the Hydra, and the Nemean Lion. She inherited her mother's hybrid form and her father's destructive temper, a perfect engine of ordeal.

myths.title: The Riddle of the Sphinx
myths.text: Sent by Hera to ravage Thebes after the city's guilt, the Sphinx settled on Mount Phicium and stopped travellers with her riddle. Those who failed she seized and devoured. Thebes was paralysed until Oedipus, the exile from Corinth, approached and answered correctly. The Sphinx, defeated by human intelligence, threw herself from the cliff.

myths.title: The Great Sphinx of Giza
myths.text: The Greek sphinx owes part of its form to Egypt, where colossal lion-bodied statues with royal human heads guarded temples and tombs for more than two thousand years before the Theban monster was conceived. The name was borrowed, but the riddle and the strangling are Greek inventions.

lore.syncretism: The Greek Sphinx merged with the much older Egyptian sphinx guardian, and the composite figure travelled through Roman, Byzantine, and Renaissance art. In medieval Europe the sphinx became a symbol of sin, especially deceit and luxury. By the Enlightenment it had become the emblem of enigma itself, and modern psychology borrowed the 'Riddle of the Sphinx' as a metaphor for the Oedipus complex.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Sphinx is one of the most durable images in world art. The Great Sphinx of Giza remains an icon of ancient Egypt, while the Greek riddling sphinx dominates literature from Sophocles to Freud. The word itself has become a verb for any mysterious or inscrutable presence. In popular culture the sphinx appears as gatekeeper, puzzle-master, and symbol of ancient wisdom, preserving the ancient idea that knowledge is the price of passage.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The Sphinx does not ask for strength or beauty; she asks for understanding. Her riddle is not a trick but a compressed account of human life: four legs, two legs, three legs. To answer is to accept mortality. Oedipus answers and so enters Thebes—and into the very fate he thought he had escaped.

The Sphinx teaches that thresholds are guarded by insight, not force. Every important transition demands that we name what we are. Those who cannot answer remain outside, devoured by their own incomprehension. The monster is not the danger; the inability to understand oneself is.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Σφίγξ, from σφίγγω, 'to squeeze, strangle'. The word was borrowed into Latin as Sphinx and into English with a short i, flattening the γξ cluster to 'nx'. PUNICODEX uses Sphigx to keep the etymological gamma-ksi cluster legible in Latin script. The Egyptian sphinx, though visually related, is a separate cultural entity with its own name and history.
